Who decides what, who advises, and who to ask. Most friction on a digital services team comes from two people who each think a decision is theirs, or from a decision nobody thinks is theirs. This page settles both.

## When

- Read it when you join the team, and before your first quarterly planning.
- Come back when a decision stalls, or when two people give a requester different answers.
- Review it at the yearly direction review, and whenever the team adds or loses a role.

## Who

- **Product manager** owns this document and keeps it current.
- **Executive steering group** approves the decision structure in it.
- Everyone on the team uses it, and so do AI agents working with the team.

## How it works

### How decisions flow

1. **Input comes from everywhere.** End users, partner staff, leaders and the community all feed in, through research, triage, the advisory group and the steering group.
2. **The steering group and product manager set direction.** Together they write the vision, strategy and goals. The steering group approves them.
3. **The product manager turns direction into a roadmap.** The product manager owns the roadmap, the priority order of Strategic work, and the Initiatives and Solutions within it.
4. **The team decides how.** The people doing the work decide how to do it, size it and commit to it.
5. **Decisions go back out.** The roadmap is open to anyone at any time. The steering group, advisory group and stakeholders hear what changed at the monthly meetings, and requesters hear back through triage.

Advice and decisions are different things. The advisory group, champions and stakeholders shape decisions. They don't make them, and they need to know that going in.

### Decision rights

| Decision | Decides | Advises | Told |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vision and strategy | Executive steering group approves; product manager drafts | Advisory group, team | Everyone |
| Goals and targets | Executive steering group with the product manager | Advisory group, UX designer and researcher | Everyone |
| Resources for a large Initiative | Executive steering group | Product manager | Team |
| Roadmap and the order of Strategic work | Product manager | Product trio, advisory group | Steering group, stakeholders |
| This quarter's capacity split | Product manager | Scrum master, technical architect, product owner | Steering group |
| Keep, change or drop a Solution | Product manager | Product trio | Advisory group, steering group |
| Order of the small request board (first in, first out by default; changes for urgency) | Product owner | Content strategist | Requesters |
| Order of Technical maintenance and bugs | Technical architect | Development team | Product manager |
| How the work is built, sizes and estimates | Development team | Technical architect, UX designer and researcher | Product owner |
| What the team commits to in a sprint | Development team | Product owner, scrum master | Product manager |
| Whether a story is done | Product owner | Development team | |
| When a Solution launches and to whom | Product manager | Product owner (readiness check), technical architect | Affected groups |
| Changing a commitment mid-quarter | Product manager with the executive steering group | Team | Advisory group |
| Future consideration or will not do for an idea | Product manager | Product owner | Requester |

The **product trio** (product manager, UX designer and researcher, and an engineer, usually the technical architect) sets the boundaries for discovery and approves what moves forward. The product manager speaks for value, the designer for usability, and the engineer for feasibility. Others are inputs. When the trio disagrees, the product manager decides and says why.

### Who to ask

| Ask | About | Example questions |
|---|---|---|
| **Product manager** | What and why | Why are we building this? Which goal does it serve? Can this wait until next quarter? |
| **Technical architect or scrum master** | How and when | How should we build this? What's blocking me? When will this be ready? |
| **Functional manager** | Performance, career and admin | Can I take this training? How am I doing? Can I take leave that week? |

A **functional manager** is the person you report to on the organization chart. On a team that works this way, your functional manager and the person who sets your priorities are often different people. That is by design. The functional manager owns your growth, performance and time off. The product manager owns the order of the work. If those pull against each other, the two of them settle it, not you.

### Who orders each kind of work

| Work type | Who puts it in order |
|---|---|
| Strategic | Product manager |
| Small requests | Product owner (first in, first out by default; steps in when urgency or priorities change) |
| Technical maintenance, including bugs | Technical architect |

Each owner works inside the capacity share set at planning. Nobody else reorders their list. If one share is running out, the owner raises it at sprint review.

### Where roles overlap

Some pairs of roles share work. The overlap is healthy when both people know who leads.

| Pair | They share | Who leads |
|---|---|---|
| Product manager and product owner | Slicing Solutions into Deliverables, writing target outcomes, talking to requesters | Product manager on what goes in Now; product owner on the backlog and stories |
| Product manager and UX designer and researcher | Discovery planning, listening sessions, deciding which Solution to test | Product manager on the decision; designer on how research is run |
| UX designer and researcher and development team | Prototypes, design readiness, accessibility checks | Designer on what people experience; developers on how it's built |
| UX designer and researcher and content strategist | Research on forms and instructions, plain language, usability tests | Designer on research; content strategist on words and Enable |
| Product owner and scrum master | Running refinement, keeping stories ready, sprint numbers | Product owner on content; scrum master on process |

### Roles across the process flow

L leads. I is involved.

| Step | Product manager | Product owner | Scrum master | UX designer and researcher | Technical architect | Development team | Content strategist | Steering group | Advisory group |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Capture ideas | L (idea log) | L (triage) | | I | I | | I | | I |
| 2. Set direction | L | | | I | I | | | L (approves) | I |
| 3. Plan the quarter | L | I | I (runs the math) | I | I | I | I | Told | Told |
| 4. Discover | L | I | | L (research) | I | I | I | | Told |
| 5. Slice the work | I | L | I | I | I | I | I | | |
| 6. Build and release | I (launch call) | L | I | I | I | L (build) | I | | |
| 7. Review the sprint | I | L (report) | L (meetings) | I | I | I | I | Told | Told |
| 8. Enable | I | I | | I | | | L | | I |

## Template

Copy this for a new team or when roles change.

| Field | What goes here |
|---|---|
| Role | Name, as used in the glossary |
| Person | Who holds it. One person can hold more than one role on a small team |
| Decides | Decisions from the table above that this role makes |
| Leads | Process steps and meetings this role leads |
| Orders | Which work list, if any |
| Ask them about | Two or three example questions |
| Functional manager | Who they report to on the organization chart |

## DMV example

The DMV digital service team, at Q1 planning.

| Role | Person | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Product manager | One, full time | Owns the roadmap and the three active Initiatives |
| Product owner | One, full time | Also runs weekly triage |
| Scrum master | Shared with another team, half time | |
| Technical architect | One | Also the team's engineering lead in the product trio |
| Development team | Three developers | |
| UX designer and researcher | One | |
| Content strategist | One | Leads Enable and the champion network |
| Executive steering group | DMV administrator, IT director, field services manager | Meets monthly |
| Advisory group | Two field office managers, a call center lead, a disability advocate, a county partner | Meets monthly |

Two decisions from the quarter, and who made them:

- **Starting staff training in parallel with the beta.** The Staff Training Program went Off track at the Sprint 3 review. The product manager heard the advisory group on Feb 18, where field office managers offered two champions. Moving the handoff date changed a commitment, so the steering group agreed it on Feb 25.
- **Fixing the payment bug the same day.** Renewal payments over $500 failed at the last step. The technical architect owns bugs, so they had a developer pick it up from Technical maintenance capacity without waiting for the product manager. The product manager heard about it at standup.

## Rules of thumb

- Every decision has one owner. "We decided together" is fine for the conversation, not for the record.
- Advice is not a vote. Tell advisors up front that they shape decisions and someone else makes them.
- Ask the right person. A priority question to a functional manager, or a performance question to the product manager, creates a second answer nobody can act on.
- One person can hold several roles on a small team. Write down which hat they're wearing when they decide.
- When two roles overlap, decide who leads before the work starts, not after it goes wrong.
- Not yet covered here: team size and shape, how committees beyond steering and advisory fit, and how AI agents take part in decisions. These are parked until the team has run a few quarters.
